I think most folks (on both sides of the argument) have no idea why CO2, in particular, is relevant and basically just pick a side and then start reciting lines from their favorite site and attack each other when questioned since they don't actually have any real understanding of the issue to debate on. So here is why CO2 is relevant!

Why CO2 Even Matters

When energy from the sun hits a planet it is absorbed and then radiated back off. Without an atmosphere this is the extent of the process. So a planet like Mercury, which is right by the sun, gets down to -279F during night time and then heats up to about 800F during the day. Things change radically with an atmosphere, but the process is not intuitive. I mean if you actually think about things, have you ever wondered why it is that atmospheres do such an incredibly good job of keeping heat in, but don't do just as good a job of keeping it out? There's a specific reason for this that is tied to the greenhouse gases, and CO2 in particular. When energy from the sun hits a planet nearly all of the energy is in the form of shortwave radiation which just means it has a short wavelength if you remember your high school physics. However, when the energy is emitted back off the planet however it's emitted almost exclusively as longwave radiation.

Now the reason CO2 is important here is that it has a unique characteristic. CO2 does not absorb shortwave radiation. But it absorbs and reemits longwave radiation. Basically what this means is that it lets the radiation from the sun in and then emits it back at the Earth when the Earth it emits it off into the atmosphere. This results in a warming scenario.

So I mentioned that Mercury gets up to 800F. Even though Venus is nearly twice as far away from the sun as Mercury, some 30 million miles, it's far far hotter. The temperature everywhere on Venus is about 860F. The reason for this is that the atmosphere there is primarily composed of CO2. It results in an insane situation where the planet is actually hotter than it would be if it was directly exposed to the sun's radiation - everywhere on the planet.

Humans?

So CO2 has an enormous influence on the temperature of a planet. So where do we come into play? The first thing that's important to understand is that CO2, prior to the industrial revolution, had been in an equilibrium cycle for hundreds of thousands of years. It had some cyclic peaks and valleys, but remained very consistent. Now the amount of CO2 that humans are adding is not large relative to the entire volume of CO2 in play in our natural atmosphere. We are adding trillions of pounds, but their is an extremely large and complex cycle of CO2 release, emission, and so forth on our planet. However, even though relative to the amounts in play, we're not adding much - when you add something to a system that's in balance you can radically change things. And that we have. This is a graph of CO2 levels over the past million years or so. We've upset an equilibrium that had lasted for hundreds of thousands of years.

I know it's fun to feed the conspiracy theories and all, but electronic parts simply can't last forever. The old incandescent light bulbs have a complex process going on inside them. The tungsten filament which glows to incandescence boils off tungsten atoms due to evaporation. The tungsten vapor then interacts with the glass bulb and gas mixture inside to form a cycle to evaporate and re-deposit the tungsten on the filament. The gas mixture inside the bulb, usually argon or nitrogen, can control the rate at which this cycle happens and allow for a longer life of the filament. It's not a perfect system and eventually the filament will thin too much in on spot and the electrical resistance will change. The bulb will then burn out the next time it is turned on due to thermal stress breaking the filament at that weak point. It's not designed to fail. It's actually designed to have as long a life as practical given its wattage, operating voltage, light output and environmental conditions. Had this not been worked out then you'd be replacing incandescent bulbs within a couple of days of the last replacement. Sure there are some bulbs that last longer like the older Edison carbonized filament bulbs but they don't produce anywhere near the light output or color spectrum of a modern tungsten filament bulb. It's a huge trade-off.

Okay, so what about LED and CFL? Well both of these technologies can have a very long life indeed. The reason they don't last as long as they could in a household light bulb is due to the electronics that drive them. LEDs can emit light for decades if they are treated right. A proper power supply that keeps their voltage and current at a steady state will let them last long enough to actually have the molecules that make up the semiconductor chip inside them to migrate out of place and eventually destroy the circuit (this happens to all semiconductors btw including CPUs). Now switch that good power supply for a crappy voltage/current divider circuit that fits inside a bulb form factor and uses run of the mill components. That power supply is going to be a mess. The power will be poorly regulated and dirty (electrical noise) and will may even not be a true DC output. This is going to affect the life span of the LED tremendously because the conditions are bad. The LED will probably survive but the components in the power supply can fail too. Same with CFLs. When the power supply dies it takes the whole thing out. It's not necessarily planned obsolescence that keeps their life down but instead the cost cutting measures of not using top notch components or a better power supply design that would increase manufacturing costs. A properly engineered LED bulb can be made to survive a very long time, but would you pay a very high (comparative) price for it and would it meet your brightness, color and size requirements? Sure it might potentially last 10 or more years, but what if even with all those engineering improvements it still dies from a power surge during a lightning storm? Now you're out a lot of money and it's no better than the cheap ones. It's easy to believe all this is simply manufacturing greed but the reality is a lot of it is just plain old engineering limitations at work. There is greed in there too, but it's just one factor.

Duty Cycle is something different. It has to do with average voltage over an period when you have a direct current source attached to a switch or digital source. The Duty Cycle is the ratio between the Switched On Time phase versus the Total Time Period available to be Switched On. The voltage will be switched between on and off. A duty cycle of 1 means it's completely on. A duty cycle of say 0.6 means its on 60% of the time and off the remaining 40%, meaning the light only gets up to 60% brightness (This is a simplified explanation).
